06-1.file: Hollerith census machine at CHM by Tomwsulcer.jpg
06-1.author: Tomwsulcer
06-1.caption: A replica of Hollerith's census tabulator at the Computer History Museum: rows of counting dials above a punched-card reader.

06-2.author: William M. Connolley
06-2.caption: William Thomson's (Lord Kelvin's) 1876 tide-predicting machine, its pulleys and wheels adding up ten tide patterns.

06-3.file: Differential analyser built for Manchester University physicists, 1935 - Science Museum, London - DSC05581.jpg
06-3.author: Daderot
06-3.caption: A 1935 differential analyser built for Manchester University on Vannevar Bush's design, with long shafts and integrators. Science Museum, London.

07-1.file: Alan Turing (1912-1954) in 1936 at Princeton University.jpg
07-1.author: Unknown photographer
07-1.caption: Alan Turing in 1936, the year his paper on imaginary computing machines was published, at Princeton University.

07-2.author: Rocky Acosta
07-2.caption: A working model of a Turing machine built by Mike Davey: a long tape runs between two reels through a read/write head.

07-3.author: Unknown authorUnknown author
07-3.caption: Portrait of Claude Shannon, who showed that switch circuits could do logic and founded information theory.

08-1.author: Venusianer at German Wikipedia
08-1.caption: The replica of Konrad Zuse's Z3 relay computer at the Deutsches Museum in Munich, with racks full of relays.

08-2.author: Capvideo
08-2.caption: Part of the Harvard Mark I (Aiken-IBM Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator) on display at Harvard's Science Center.

08-3.author: User:Manop
08-3.caption: A replica of the Atanasoff-Berry Computer at Iowa State University, with its vacuum tubes, memory drum and control panel.

09-1.file: National WWII Museum Dec 2015 - Enigma machine up close.jpg
09-1.author: ironypoisoning
09-1.caption: An Enigma machine at the National WWII Museum: rotor wheels at the top, lamps, keys, and the plugboard with cables in front.

09-2.author: Mike McBey
09-2.caption: The rebuilt Colossus codebreaking computer at The National Museum of Computing, Bletchley Park, with its tape reader on the left.

09-3.file: The Bombe in Bletchley Park in 2022.jpg
09-3.author: Vintage Fan 5678
09-3.caption: The rebuilt Turing-Welchman Bombe at Bletchley Park, with rows of coloured spinning drums that copied Enigma rotors.

10-1.file: Glen Beck and Betty Snyder program the ENIAC in building 328 at the Ballistic Research Laboratory.jpg
10-1.author: Unknown authorUnknown author
10-1.caption: Glen Beck and Betty Snyder program ENIAC among its cable-covered panels, in a U.S. Army photo from the 1940s.

10-2.author: Unidentified U.S. Army photographer
10-2.caption: ENIAC programmers Betty Jennings (left) and Frances Bilas (right) at the main control panel, preparing for its 1946 debut.

10-3.author: Logg Tandy
10-3.caption: Surviving ENIAC panels on display at the University of Pennsylvania, with a portable function table on the left.
